result: A linear regression model was developed to estimate readthrough propensity (RTP) for all human stop codon contexts by formalizing 15-nucleotide stop codon contexts (SCCs) as 51-dimensional binary vectors and calculating regression coefficients from 66 experimentally measured basal translational readthrough (BTR) values from human nonsense mutations.
evaluation: Claims C2, C31-C46 describe the development and initial application of the computational model. The methodology is clearly described with appropriate data sources (nonsense mutations providing unbiased contexts), mathematical formalization (binary vectors, linear regression), and genome-wide application. The approach is logically sound and the model parameters are specified.

result: Experimental validation using a dual reporter assay (Venus-SCC-hRluc) confirmed that the algorithm predicts BTR, with tested candidates showing readthrough between 0.10% and 2.91%, and geneticin increasing readthrough 3.25 to 40.38-fold, with maximal BTR limited to below 15%.
evaluation: Claims C47-C59 describe experimental validation of the computational predictions. The dual reporter assay design is appropriate for measuring BTR (excludes introns, RNA structures), controls are adequate (geneticin induction, fusion protein without stop), and quantification method is sound (luciferase/Venus ratio). The range of readthrough values and geneticin response validate the assay and support the BTR concept.

result: Iterative model refinement (LINiter) incorporating additional experimental data achieved a correlation of 0.34 (p=0.002), and analysis of regression coefficients indicated that nucleotides following the stop codon contribute most to readthrough.
evaluation: Claims C60-C68 describe model refinement and initial analysis. The iterative approach is sound, incorporating new experimental data. The correlation coefficient is weak but statistically significant, which is reasonable given the complexity of the biological process. The observation about nucleotide contributions is supported by the regression coefficient analysis shown in figures.

result: Feature selection identified that the stop codon and three nucleotides immediately downstream (positions +4 to +6) have the largest influence on BTR, yielding the consensus motif UGA CUA (LINfs3 model) with improved correlation of 0.41 (p=0.0001).
evaluation: Claims C3, C33, C64-C71 describe the derivation of the consensus motif through feature selection. The methodology is appropriate (successive elimination of low-contribution positions), the LINfs3 model shows improved performance over LINiter, and the consensus motif is clearly defined. The statistical improvement supports the validity of the reduced model.

result: Experimental validation of the LINfs3 consensus in multiple cell types confirmed that sequences matching UGA CUA show high BTR (AQP4: 2.29%, SYTL2: 0.99%, CACNA2D4: 0.61%) compared to non-matching sequences (DHX38: 0.27%), with consistent relative rankings across HeLa, HT1080, HEK, and U373 cells.
evaluation: Claims C72-C81 provide experimental validation of the consensus motif across multiple cell types. The experimental design is appropriate (comparing sequences that match vs. don't match the consensus), results are consistent across cell types (supporting that BTR is a property of the SCC), and the data support the predictive value of the LINfs3 consensus. The observation of position +7 contribution is a reasonable inference from the data.

result: A machine learning-based PTS1 prediction algorithm was adapted from plants to humans using orthology searches on 24 known human PTS1 sequences, and applied to predict PTS1 posterior probabilities for all predicted readthrough extensions in the human transcriptome.
evaluation: Claims C4, C86-C99 describe the development and application of the PTS1 prediction algorithm. The approach is well-documented with appropriate data sources (known PTS1 proteins, orthology searches), established methodology (machine learning, previously validated in plants), and clear application to the readthrough extensions. The rationale for focusing on PTS1 is sound given their C-terminal location and prevalence.

result: LDHB was identified at the top (rank 1 of 42,069) of the genome-wide screen based on the product of RTP and PTS1 scores, with the score dropping by 50% over the first 40 transcripts, indicating LDHB has uniquely high combined readthrough and peroxisomal targeting potential.
evaluation: Claims C5, C100-C102 describe the identification of LDHB from the computational screen. The combined scoring approach (RTP × PTS1) is logical for identifying functional readthrough with peroxisomal targeting. The ranking and score distribution support LDHB as an exceptional candidate. The computational prediction is clearly documented and forms the basis for subsequent experimental validation.

result: Experimental validation confirmed LDHB has high BTR of 1.55% (±0.09%), which is strongly dependent on the stop codon context (mutations in stop codon or +4 position suppress readthrough), can be induced by geneticin to 4.38%, and occurs in full-length LDHB protein.
evaluation: Claims C103-C109 provide experimental validation of LDHB readthrough. Multiple complementary assays are used (dual reporter, Western blot with dual tags), appropriate controls are included (stop codon and context mutations), and results are consistent across assays. The 1.55% readthrough is substantial and the mutational analysis confirms the importance of the SCC, supporting the computational predictions.

result: YFP-LDHBx localizes to peroxisomes after cytosol removal, and this localization is dependent on both the PTS1 (SRL) in the extension (mutations SSI or ΔL block targeting) and the leaky UGA stop codon (UAA reduces targeting), confirming readthrough-dependent peroxisomal import.
evaluation: Claims C6, C114-C129 demonstrate peroxisomal localization of LDHBx through multiple lines of evidence. The experimental approach (cytosol removal to reveal low-abundance peroxisomal protein) is innovative and appropriate. Controls are comprehensive (YFP alone, ACOX3-PTS1 positive control, PTS1 mutations, stop codon mutations, UGG replacement). The dependence on both PTS1 and stop codon strongly supports readthrough-dependent targeting.

result: Endogenous LDHB localizes to peroxisomes in multiple cell types (HeLa, fibroblasts, COS-7, U118, rat cardiomyocytes) after cytosol removal, consistent with ~1.6% readthrough-dependent targeting, and geneticin treatment increases peroxisomal LDHBx levels (1.89-fold, p<0.0001).
evaluation: Claims C130-C137 extend the findings to endogenous LDHB across multiple cell types. The immunofluorescence approach with cytosol removal is consistent with the overexpression studies. The correspondence between measured readthrough (~1.6%) and peroxisomal localization is compelling. Testing across diverse cell types and species strengthens the conclusion. The geneticin induction of endogenous peroxisomal LDHB provides additional validation.

result: LDHB readthrough ranges from 1.55-1.88% in most cell types tested (HeLa, HEK, COS-7) but is elevated to 5.09% in U118 glioblastoma cells, suggesting LDHB stop suppression is not tissue-restricted but may be differentially regulated.
evaluation: Claims C138-C143 examine cell-type variation in LDHB readthrough. The experimental approach is appropriate (same dual reporter construct in different cell types). The finding of elevated readthrough in U118 cells is interesting and statistically robust. The conclusion that readthrough may be differentially regulated is reasonable but speculative. The data support that LDHB readthrough occurs broadly but with potential cell-type-specific modulation.

result: Phylogenetic analysis shows the PTS1 extension (SRL) is exclusively and strictly conserved in mammals but not in non-mammalian vertebrates, supporting evolutionarily conserved peroxisomal targeting of LDHBx in mammals.
evaluation: Claims C8, C144-C145 provide evolutionary evidence for functional importance. The phylogenetic analysis is appropriate and clearly presented in Figure 9. The exclusive conservation in mammals is striking and supports functional significance. The alignment quality metrics strengthen the conclusion. This evolutionary conservation provides strong independent support for the functional importance of the readthrough extension.

result: LDHBx can co-import LDHA into peroxisomes in a PTS1-dependent manner, as demonstrated by YFP-LDHA peroxisomal localization when co-expressed with CFP-LDHBx[TGG] but not alone, and this co-import is blocked by PTS1 mutations (SSI or ΔL).
evaluation: Claims C7, C146-C154 demonstrate co-import of LDHA by LDHBx. The experimental design (two-hybrid-like assay adapted from previous work) is appropriate for testing oligomer import. Controls are adequate (LDHA alone, PTS1 mutations). The results clearly show PTS1-dependent co-import. This extends the functional significance by showing that multiple LDH isoforms can access peroxisomes through LDHBx.

result: Structural modeling of the LDH-1 tetramer shows the LDHBx extension (7 additional amino acids beyond 3 unresolved amino acids) protrudes from the tetramer distal to protomer-interaction sites, confirming oligomerization is not hampered and the PTS1 is accessible for PEX5 binding.
evaluation: Claims C155-C158 provide structural support for the co-import findings. The modeling approach is appropriate (using existing crystal structure). The conclusions about extension location and accessibility are reasonable inferences from the structure. This provides mechanistic support for how oligomeric LDH can be imported with the PTS1 extension, though it is a computational model rather than experimental structure.

result: Peroxisomal LDH likely contributes to redox equivalent regeneration for β-oxidation, as the 1.6% readthrough corresponds to 1.5-2% LDH activity previously found in peroxisomes, and peroxisomes require NAD+ regeneration but the pathway has been unclear.
evaluation: Claims C9, C37, C172-C187 propose a functional role for peroxisomal LDH in redox metabolism. The correspondence between measured readthrough and historical peroxisomal LDH activity measurements is compelling (C172). The metabolic rationale is sound (peroxisomes need NAD+ regeneration, are impermeable to NAD+/NADH). However, this remains speculative as no direct functional experiments (e.g., measuring NAD+/NADH ratios, β-oxidation rates, metabolic flux) are performed. The conclusion is a reasonable hypothesis but requires experimental validation.

result: Ribosome profiling, phylogenetic approaches, and RTP screening are complementary methods for identifying readthrough, as only one of 42 genes found by ribosome profiling contains the UGA CUA consensus, suggesting multiple molecular mechanisms cause readthrough in mammals.
evaluation: Claims C83-C85 compare different approaches for identifying readthrough. The Venn diagram analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) clearly shows limited overlap between methods. The observation that different methods identify different genes is well-supported. The conclusion that multiple mechanisms exist is a reasonable inference from the data, though the claim could be strengthened by more detailed mechanistic analysis of the differences.

result: LDHBx represents a new LDH isoform generated by basal translational readthrough that affects intracellular distribution, is expressed across tissues, and exemplifies a new mechanism of post-transcriptional diversification of the genome's coding potential in mammals.
evaluation: Claims C163, C167-C171 synthesize the findings into broader conclusions. The characterization of LDHBx as a new isoform is well-supported by the experimental data (readthrough, peroxisomal localization, co-import capability). The evidence for expression across tissues is strong (multiple cell types, phylogenetic conservation). The claim about post-transcriptional diversification is a reasonable interpretation of the findings, representing a significant conceptual advance.

result: Aminoglycoside antibiotics will increase LDHB readthrough and peroxisome import of LDHBx as a pharmacological effect.
evaluation: Claim C196 identifies a pharmacological implication. This is directly supported by experimental data showing geneticin increases both readthrough in reporter assays (C55, C106, C141) and endogenous peroxisomal LDHBx levels (C136). The conclusion is well-supported and has potential clinical relevance given the common use of aminoglycosides.

result: Both fungi and mammals use stop codon suppression to localize glycolytic enzymes to peroxisomes, suggesting translational readthrough and PTS1 evolve easily to divert a constant, low fraction of enzymes to coordinate redox processes between cytosol and peroxisomes.
evaluation: Claims C191-C195 propose evolutionary and mechanistic hypotheses. The observation of convergent evolution (fungi and mammals using readthrough for peroxisomal targeting of glycolytic enzymes) is well-supported by citations (C26, C190). However, the hypotheses about ease of evolution (C192) and coordination of redox processes (C195) are speculative and not directly tested. These are reasonable hypotheses that warrant future investigation but lack experimental support in this study.

result: The elevated LDHB readthrough in U118 glioblastoma cells (~5%) suggests differential regulation of readthrough in different tissues, potentially related to cancer-associated dysregulation (Warburg effect), higher peroxisome abundance, or glial-specific metabolic demands.
evaluation: Claims C197-C201 propose explanations for the elevated readthrough in U118 cells. The observation of elevated readthrough is well-supported (C140), but the mechanistic explanations are entirely speculative. No experiments test Warburg effect involvement, peroxisome abundance, or glial-specific metabolism. These are reasonable hypotheses for future work but remain unvalidated. The claim acknowledges uncertainty ('Future experiments will show').

result: The computational approach based on formalizing SCCs and linear regression with unbiased nonsense mutation sequences is limited to 6 nucleotides before/after the stop codon, excluding extended RNA structures, but the identification of the LINfs3 consensus justifies this approach.
evaluation: Claims C210-C215 describe and justify the computational approach. The methodology is clearly described with appropriate acknowledgment of limitations (excludes RNA structures, limited sequence window). The use of nonsense mutations provides unbiased training data (C212). The successful identification of a functional consensus motif (LINfs3) that predicts experimental readthrough validates the approach despite its limitations. The self-critical assessment strengthens the work.

result: The LINfs3 consensus motif UGA CUA (with possible contribution from positions +7 and -6) is distinct from viral/yeast consensus but resembles alphavirus contexts, is found 30 times in the human genome (UGA CUA G), and has been independently validated for high readthrough.
evaluation: Claims C216-C224 characterize the consensus motif and compare it to previous findings. The motif derivation is well-supported by feature selection analysis. The genome-wide frequency is documented. The comparison to other organisms (distinct from yeast/viruses, similar to alphavirus) provides context. Independent validation by Loughran et al. (C221) strengthens confidence. The clinical relevance example (LAMA3, C224) adds translational significance.

result: The UGA CUA consensus motif causes non-linear contribution to RTP, and the better performance of LINfs3 over LINiter indicates compact linear models should be preferred with current dataset size, though larger datasets will enable non-linear models.
evaluation: Claims C225-C229 provide methodological insights about model performance and future directions. The observation that LINfs3 outperforms LINiter (C226) is supported by correlation data. The conclusion about preferring compact models with limited data is statistically sound. The predictions about future model development (C228-C229) are reasonable extrapolations. This represents good scientific practice in acknowledging current limitations and future opportunities.

result: LDHBx (1.6% readthrough, UGA CUA G context, 18-nucleotide extension) represents prototypical BTR independent of cis-factors, contrasting with VEGF-Ax which requires distant cis-elements, though PTR and BTR are not mutually exclusive as shown by OPRK1/OPRL1 achieving >30% readthrough through combined mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C230-C237 position LDHB readthrough within the broader context of readthrough mechanisms. The characterization of LDHB as BTR is well-supported by the short extension length and SCC-dependence. The comparison with VEGF-Ax (C233, C235) is appropriately cited. The acknowledgment that mechanisms can combine (C236-C237) shows nuanced understanding. This provides important conceptual framework for understanding readthrough diversity.

result: Systematic analysis of translational readthrough in humans is beginning, and combining in silico modeling, ribosome profiling, phylogenetic methods, and mass spectrometry will help identify the complete 'extensome' of readthrough-extended proteins in mammals.
evaluation: Claims C238-C239 provide perspective on the field and future directions. The assessment that systematic analysis is beginning is supported by recent literature (C159, C202-C206). The proposal to combine multiple methods is logical given the complementary nature of approaches demonstrated in this study (C83). This represents appropriate forward-looking discussion, though the prediction about identifying the complete extensome is necessarily speculative.
